newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks seen rising but Moody's a concern.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks seen rising but Moody's a concern.

text.p: Government measures to shake up the troubled Thai finance and property sectors are expected to help battered Thai stocks move up in the near term, analysts said on Thursday.
But a negative factor hanging over the stock market is the review by Moody's Investor Services, due in two months time, on whether to downgrade Thailand's long term debt ratings, they added.

The market index reached a 58-month-low last Thursday of 676.65. Some analysts expect the index to rise to the 760-point level if it builds on a recovery staged in the past four trading days after last week's drastic finance sector revamp.
In a major shake-up, authorities ordered 10 ailing finance firms to boost their capital and told financial institutions to raise provisions for sub-standard loans.
Banks and finance companies are estimated to have loaned up to 800 billion baht ($30.7 billion) to the depressed property sector, and analysts said a large portion could be bad loans.
The bourse regained composure after the cabinet approved this week the flotation of 100 billion baht in zero-coupon bonds to raise funds to bail out the property sector.

"Although the funds aren't much when compared to the amount of loans extended by banks and finance firms to property developers, they will help boost investment," said analyst Bunsom Kesapradist of Asia Credit.
"The index is expected to climb to the 760-point level in the near term. I think the index won't fall below 700 points in the foreseeable future," he added.
Funds raised through the seven-year bonds will be loaned to property developers at market interest rates so that they are able to meet their debt obligations.

Analysts said stricter fiscal discipline adopted by the government -- the cabinet last week approved 106 billion baht in spending cuts for fiscal 1996/1997 (October/September) -- also helped investor confidence.
"The government decision to slash the budget is considered positive. Investors believe it will help narrow the c/a deficit," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.
Thailand's 1996 current account deficit was eight percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and expectations are that it will narrow to 7.1-7.2 percent of GDP this year.
Thanawat said the prices of most stocks, especially finance issues, were now lower than book value.
He said the market price-earnings ratio now stood at 10.7 times compared to 31.49 times on January 4, 1994, when the index hit its peak of 1753.73.

"The Moody's recommendation is expected to be known within the next two months, which is quite far away. Right now investors are accumulating stocks and they will probably sell if the recommendation is negative," Bunsom said.
